title: Neuroethics and neurotechnology
stage: College neuroscience and cognitive science degree
audience: a college student in a neuroscience, cognitive science, psychology or biology degree program, or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Learn the ethical, legal and social questions raised by brain science and neurotechnology: research ethics with people and animals, consent and capacity, incidental findings, brain–computer interfaces and neural implants, neurostimulation and enhancement, mental privacy and neural data, neuroscience in the courtroom, free will and responsibility, brain death and disorders of consciousness, psychiatric neurosurgery and identity, and the governance of neurotechnology, with each main position presented fairly.

weeks.2: Research ethics with people: consent, capacity and incidental findings
weeks.9: Brain death and disorders of consciousness
weeks.10: Psychiatric neurosurgery, deep brain stimulation and identity
weeks.11: Governing neurotechnology: laws, standards and principles
weeks.12: Public communication of neuroscience and neuromyths

blocks.deliverable: Review a supplied consent form against the main principles.
Analyze the risks and benefits of an implanted device.
Write a balanced analysis of an enhancement question.
Week 7 midterm; evaluate a legal use of brain evidence.
Analyze a supplied case of a patient with a disorder of consciousness.
Write a policy brief on neural data.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Neuroethics brief: write a 3,000-word analysis of one neurotechnology (for example a consumer EEG headset, a brain–computer interface or deep brain stimulation for depression), covering the science, the benefits and risks, the main ethical positions in their strongest form, the current law as of the course date, and a recommendation with its strongest objection.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
